titleStmt.title: LAG-based Analysis Techniques for Scheduling Multiprocessor Hard Real-Time Sporadic DAGs

analytic.title: LAG-based Analysis Techniques for Scheduling Multiprocessor Hard Real-Time Sporadic DAGs

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Global scheduling of real time tasks with precedence constraints has received significant attention recently. Specifically, on multiprocessor systems, the directed acyclic graph (DAG) model well-represents parallelizable workloads with precedence constraints. Hence, many studies have recently been published analyzing DAG structures using decomposition and windowbased analysis methods. We identified a set of schedulable DAG taskets that are hard-to-analyze using state-of-the-art windowbased schedulability tests. Additionally, we observe that the window-based test solely depends on one structural feature of the DAG taskset, which raises concerns about its pessimism in many settings. In this paper, to address these concerns, for hard real-time sporadic implicit-deadline DAG tasksets, we perform LAG-based schedulability analysis, which offers a more holistic view of the taskset than the window-based analysis. We present a companion utilization-based schedulability test to the state-ofthe-art, which considers additional structural features of DAGs. Our results show that by considering such features, our LAGbased test empirically dominates the state-of-the-art test on over 80% of the evaluated DAG tasksets. Moreover, combining our LAG-based test in conjunction with the window-based tests can achieve high schedulability in many cases.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Recent works utilize seminal window-based analysis [1] to propose schedulability tests which provide apriori scheduling guarantees for hard real-time (HRT) task systems considering various complexities, including sporadic, mixed-criticality, suspension, and precedence constraints [1]- [11]. A key intuition in window-based methods is to analyze the maximum workload in a specific time window on a multiprocessor and bound it to guarantee schedulability. However, considering multiple complex task features may yield laxer bounds on the maximum workload, leading to considerable and perhaps unnecessary pessimism in the resulting schedulability tests.

On the other hand, LAG-based analysis, which historically has been used to find tardiness bounds in soft real-time (SRT) systems, has recently been used to analyze task models under the HRT setting, which contain features known to be hard to analyze using window-based analysis such as self-suspending tasks [12] and GANG tasks [13]. This motivated us to explore the feasibility of improving the existing schedulability tests of other HRT systems utilizing LAG-based analysis. A key difference between the LAG-based and the window-based analysis is that the LAG-based approach offers a more holistic view of the system by comparing the allocated execution time for all the tasks by a target scheduler to a hypotheticalprocessor share scheduler. Hence we believe the LAG-based approach may remarkably improve utilization bounds on more generalized policies such as global scheduling (compared to partitioned scheduling).

One such application is the global scheduling of tasksets with precedence constraints, which has recently seen much interest from researchers [4], [10], [14]- [37]. Many real-world applications in real-time and embedded systems contain abstract constructs such as directed-acyclic graphs (DAGs) [38] to represent such precedent constraints. Prior works [16]- [20], [23]- [25] provide resource augmentation-based schedulability tests by decomposing the DAG task. However, they do not consider a specific policy for prioritization between various subtasks in a DAG. Instead, they leave the prioritization between various subtasks to the underlying scheduler that schedules the decomposed tasks. The Lazy-Cpath policy [4] represents a recently developed intra-DAG scheduling policy that prioritizes sub-tasks in a DAG that are not on its critical path over subtasks on the critical path. Intuitively, this policy is a relatively low-cost method to define a better order of execution among a DAG's subtasks. Combined with the window-based analysis, a utilization-based schedulability test is formulated for a GEDF scheduler with the Lazy-Cpath policy on HRT sporadic DAGs [4]. Key motivation. As discussed and empirically observed in the state-of-the-art window-based schedulability test for DAG taskset [4], analyzing the schedulability of DAG task systems with high C/T Ratio could yield unacceptable pessimism and thus remains largely an open problem. The C/T Ratio (r) for a DAG taskset is defined as the minimum workload that a DAG in the taskset has to have on its critical path as a fraction of the DAG's total workload. Hence for every DAG in the taskset, its critical path workload should be ≥ r × its total workload (more formally defined in Section II). Intuitively, the C/T Ratio represents the parallelization factor of a DAG taskset, i.e., a higher C/T Ratio corresponds to a lower parallelization and branching factor. Therefore, [4] makes an intuitive claim that a DAG taskset with lower C/T Ratio is more straightforward to schedule from both runtime and analytical perspectives due to higher flexibility. So, analyzing the schedulability of DAG taskset with high C/T Ratio remains largely open that the seminal window-based analysis is unable to handle. Intuitively, the window-based analysis naturally underperforms for such settings since analyzing carry-in workloads for a specific window with tasks containing long sequential chains (due to high C/T Ratio) leads to unnecessary pessimism.

To address these challenges, in this paper, we present the first LAG-based analysis for the HRT sporadic implicit deadline DAG taskset under CP-EDF (GEDF with Lazy-Cpath policy). We believe LAG-based analysis, naturally, may be a better base analytical framework for handling the abovementioned hard case where DAG tasksets have a high C/T Ratio. Our intuition is the following: since LAG-based analysis compares the progress made by a scheduler with a hypothetical ideal scheduler, it offers a more aggregated view of the system that would enable it to well-handle the hard high C/T Ratio case. Related works. There has been considerable research on various scheduling policies and schedulability analysis of HRT DAG task systems [16]- [27]. A section of prior work concentrate only on systems containing a single DAG task [26], [27], with limited extensibility to multi-DAG systems. Many works use decomposition techniques to convert DAGs to single standalone tasks with various offsets and deadlines to maintain the dependency constraints [16]- [20], [23]- [25]. These tasks are then passed on to traditional schedulers. It has been proven by V. Bonifaci et al. [25] that a decomposition-based approach cannot produce a resource augmentation better than 2 -1 m under GEDF. The most recent work by F. Guan et al. [19] provide a DAG-Fluid algorithm with an augmentation bound of 2 -1 m+1 assuming fractional execution and preemption. There are also several utilization-based schedulability tests for HRT systems with a DAG taskset [4], [10], [20]. Out of all these utilization-based schedulability tests, the test by Z. Dong et al. [4] empirically dominate all of them (to a noticeable degree) by using a GEDF scheduler running the Lazy-Cpath policy.

Our contributions. This paper presents the first LAG-based analysis on HRT sporadic implicit deadline DAG task systems under CP-EDF (GEDF with Lazy-Cpath policy). We develop a utilization-based schedulability test for the DAG task system. Compared to prior closed-form schedulability tests for implicit deadline sporadic DAG tasksets from [4], [16], [19], [20], [23]- [25], our schedulability test incorporates a component that is solely dependant on a key structural feature of DAGs, the parallelism of a DAG across its makespan. This makes our test incomparable to the previous schedulability tests. Intuitively, incorporating such a component into a closed-form test helps analyze complex scenarios like the DAG tasksets with a high C/T Ratio while introducing a trade-off where some DAG tasksets, even with very low total utilization, could fail the structural test. However, our empirical studies show structures that fail our test are in a significant minority. Specifically, our LAG-based test empirically outperforms the current empirically-dominant state-of-the-art schedulability test [4] on over 80% of all the DAG tasksets generated, especially on DAG tasksets with sparse edge density, and/or medium U sum , and/or high C/T Ratio. However, [4] outperforms our approach on DAG tasksets that exhibit high edge density and low C/T Ratio. Furthermore, our results show that for specific settings, the tasksets passed by both tests are distinct. Hence, using our test along with the windowbased test, we can provide very high schedulability on sporadic DAG tasksets in many cases, as proven by our results. Thus, this paper offers a non-trivial LAG-based analysis which augments/improves classical window-based analysis by analyzing hard-to-handle DAG tasksets.

div.p: A. Lazy-Cpath Policy [4] Under the Lazy-Cpath policy, at any time instance, among all the ready jobs in τ i , the jobs of the subtasks on Cpath i have the lowest priority. GEDF with the Lazy-Cpath policy works as follows: at each time instant, the scheduler first tries to schedule ready jobs with the earliest deadlines; if the number of such ready jobs is more than m, then GEDF first schedules ready jobs of subtasks that are not on Cpath i . Let CP-EDF denote the scheduling strategy after applying the Lazy-Cpath policy to GEDF. Subtask jobs with dependencies are ready-to-execute only if all its dependencies are complete. Additionally, if subtasks do not execute till their WCET, the critical path might not be the path with the highest workload in a DAG task. Under such conditions ease of analysis of the Lazy-Cpath policy is lost, hence we assume that the execution time of each node is equal to its WCET. Such an assumption is commonplace in deriving schedulability tests for HRT systems, as evidenced by its requirement in prior studies [4] (especially for analysis that use carry-in jobs [39], [40]). We can enforce practically such an assumption by making an early finishing subtask wait till its WCET.

div.head: III. ANALYSIS
div.p: This section develops a new utilization-based schedulability test by applying LAG-based reasoning to the DAG task system under CP-EDF.

div.head: A. LAG-based analysis for DAG tasks.
div.p: Definition 13 (Executing and non-executing critical path intervals). Under CP-EDF a time interval [t 1 , t 2 ), where t 2 > t 1 , is considered to be an executing critical path interval for τ i if there exists at least one job of a subtask t k i ∈ Cpath i that is executing throughout the interval; otherwise, it is considered to be a non-executing critical path interval for τ i .

This executing/non-executing critical path interval analysis takes advantage of the following key fact (which follows from Lemma 2): if a DAG job τ i,j is released but does not execute a critical path subtask, all the m processors were busy during this interval.

We perform LAG-based analysis for a DAG taskset τ . Say, at least one job of τ misses its deadlines under CP-EDF. A valid PS schedule exists for τ as long as U sum ≤ m. Let t d be the first time instant where a deadline miss happens and τ p be the task that misses its deadline at t d . We can ignore the tasks with a deadline greater than t d as they do not impact the execution of τ p .

div.p: Proof. We prove by contradiction. Assume an instance of τ , for which Eqs. 10 and 11 hold, but under CP-EDF one or more jobs of τ miss the deadline. div.p: We can observe that for DAG tasksets with C/T Ratio = 1, the following conditions holds:

div.p: Hence, Eq. 11 always holds and our LAG-based test converts to the classical density test [41] given by:

div.p: we can observe that the window-based test considers only one structural feature of DAG tasksets, the fraction of workload on the critical path. In comparison, decomposition-based methods [16], [19], [20], [23]- [25], consider structural features of DAGs for converting them into individual tasks. However, their closed-form schedulability tests represented by the capacity and resource augmentation bounds only depend upon U sum and σ max . Hence the schedulability test from the capacity and resource augmentation bounds results in significant pessimism, as evidenced by the dominance of the window-based test over them in the results from [4]. In comparison, our test takes into consideration the parallelism of a DAG across its makespan (using Eq. 11) along with the fraction of workload on the critical path. However, considering these additional structural features could also lead to pessimism in certain cases. In the next section, we present our empirical results, which show that structures that negatively affect our test are in a significant minority compared to the structures that are beneficial to Eq. 11. And by considering these additional structural features, our test can resolve the hard to analyze settings. Still, for the highest schedulability results, our test should be used in conjunction with the test from the window-based analysis given by Eq. 22.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTS
div.p: In this section, we present a comparison between the utilization-based schedulability tests from the LAG-based and window-based analysis. For this purpose, we generate multiple DAGs with varying structures using standard randomized methods used in prior studies.

div.head: A. Experimental Setup
div.p: In this section, we detail the generation of DAG tasksets. As a starting point, we use the Erdos-Renyi method [42], which generates a DAG G based on two parameters number of nodes (n) and probability (ρ), representing the probability of an edge.

As discussed earlier, we are concerned with the schedulability of DAG tasksets having a specific C/T Ratio. So we need to distribute the execution time such that this ratio is maintained for the whole taskset. To achieve this, first, we get a random period p ∈ [1000, 70000]. Then given the total utilization of the DAG task as u, we know the total execution units needed to be distributed over the nodes as C = u × p . We check if C ≥ 1000; if not, we choose a suitably large period such that this condition is valid. Then we generate nodes representing the subtasks having an execution time selected as an integer between [ 0.001C , 0.2C ] until the sum of the costs of all nodes equals C. We set the value of n equal to the number of nodes generated. Then we apply the Erdos-Renyi method to generate the dependencies using the values n, ρ. If the resulting graph is disconnected, we add a minimum number of edges between the connected components; while ensuring no cycles are formed. To achieve this, we perform a topological ordering, and the new edges are always from nodes with a lower index to a higher index. Then we identify the Cpath of the constructed graph and compute the len(Cpath). If len(Cpath) < C × r, then we keep adding nodes to the critical path by adding new edges, such that they ensure the number of nodes lying on the Cpath keeps increasing until len(Cpath) ≥ C × r. This can be achieved again by using topological ordering. Starting from the end of the order, keep adding the nodes that do not lie on the Cpath until we reach the order's top. If all nodes are added to the Cpath, then the critical fraction for that DAG will be equal to 1 and len(Cpath) becomes equal to C, hence len(Cpath) ≥ C × r is guaranteed to be valid.
Further, we define modes of generation for three crucial parameters that control the overall DAG taskset. These parameters are as follows:
• Each DAG's total utilization, u.
• Probability of an edge between two nodes in a DAG, ρ.

• C/T Ratio. For u, similar to the evaluation in [4], we define three modes of generation to capture the various types of DAG tasksets and their effect on the schedulability tests. The three modes are as follows:

Note that if the remaining utilization in a taskset (to produce a particular U sum ) is below the selection range in medium and heavy modes, then a single DAG task out of the selection range is added to the taskset. Next, for the probability of an edge ρ, we define the following three modes:
div.formula: • Sparse ρ ∈ (0, 0.1]. • Normal ρ ∈ (0, 0.5]. • Dense ρ ∈ (0, 0.7].
div.p: These three modes produce DAGs with different edge densities. And as stated before, we ensure the generated DAGs are connected, i.e., no node/nodes are isolated. We limit the highest ρ in our studies to 0.7, as higher ρ makes DAGs constructed from Erdos-Renyi method similar to a tree structure (with edges between all nodes). Hence, to ensure that the generated DAGs are realistic in our studies, we limit ρ to the above three modes. Next, for C/T Ratio, we have the following modes:
div.formula: • Light, C/T Ratio ∈ [0.4, 0.6]. • Medium, C/T Ratio ∈ [0.6, 0.8].
div.p: • Heavy, C/T Ratio ∈ [0.8, 1]. We limit the lowest value of the C/T Ratio to 0.4, as a lower C/T Ratio makes the DAG very distributed, which is not realistic. Additionally, since C/T Ratio is the minimum critical fraction of a DAG in the taskset, having lower values loosens the constraints on generated DAG tasksets making individual settings less specific.

div.head: B. Experimental Results
div.p: This section presents our results for both LAG-based and window-based utilization tests on the generated tasksets. As stated before, our test is intended to be used in conjunction with the test from the window-based analysis. So for every scenario, we present three values, namely the LAG-based (our approach), Window-based (State-of-the-art), and combined, which takes a logical OR between the two tests. We perform two studies to capture their behavior in which we plot the average schedulability of 1000 tasksets generated for each setting with m = 8. The first study is on the behavior of schedulability tests vs. U sum /m under various modes of all the variables listed above. The second study is on the behavior of schedulability tests vs. C/T Ratio under fixed U sum and various modes for u and ρ.

The first study of the schedulability tests vs. U sum /m under various settings for u, ρ, and C/T Ratio is presented in Figures As the edge density of DAGs decreases, ND set for each subtask τ k i on the Cpath of τ i becomes larger; hence Eq. 11 is much more probable to hold in such tasksets. Furthermore, a high C/T Ratio ensures a high critical fraction ( σi ui ), increasing the left part of the bound while simultaneously decreasing the right part. We also observe that our LAG-based test is significantly better than the state-of-theart Window-based analysis for tasksets under all settings with U sum /m > 0.3.

This study shows that our test can achieve significantly higher schedulability by considering additional DAG structural features, especially for lower edge density settings. Since the window-based test is blind to DAG structural features other than the ratio of workload on the critical path, the schedulability of the window-based test remains almost constant across DAG tasksets generated for different edge densities for the same u and C/T Ratio (Figures 345). Such behavior is counterintuitive as DAG tasksets with higher edge density represent subtasks with more precedence constraints leading to lower parallelism.

Our second study is on the behavior of schedulability tests vs. C/T Ratio under specific U sum settings. From our first study, we observe that for U sum /m ∈ [0.2, 0.6], the behavior of two schedulability tests is interesting. Hence, Figures 6-10 present our second study for U sum /m ∈ [0.2, 0.6] (with a step of 0.1). Similar to the first study, each figure presents nine lines, which correspond to the three values: LAG-based, Window-based, and combined under the three edge density settings. Figure 6 presents the results for U sum = 1.6, in which we observe that for u = Light, our LAG-based test significantly outperforms the window-based approach under the Sparse edge density setting. Furthermore, under every edge density setting, our LAG-based approach achieves perfect schedulability as C/T Ratio approaches one which matches the expected behavior of a test that converges to the classical density test from our observations in Section III-B. Hence our LAG-based approach rectifies this critical behavioral flaw in the window-based test. Similarly, for u = Medium and Heavy, our test outperforms the window-based test under Sparse edge density setting. But, for Normal, Dense ρ settings, our test only dominates for higher C/T Ratio. Figure 7 presents the behavior of the schedulability test for U sum = 2.4; compared to U sum = 1.6, the window-based test performs worse, and the LAG-based test is more dominant under all settings except for scenarios having u = Light, high edge density, and low C/T Ratio. However, as the density of edges increases, our LAG-based test performs worse than the window-based tests (for Normal and Dense settings) especially when the U sum is low for all u settings. And as the U sum increases, the LAG-based test starts to dominate the state-of-the-art window-based test for all u setting, even for DAGs with higher edge densities. Specifically for u = Light, our test starts dominating under all edge density settings for U sum /m > 0.3. Similarly, for u = Medium, U sum /m > 0.25 and u = Heavy, U sum /m > 0.2 our LAG-based test achieves higher schedulability under every edge density setting. For Figure 4, which presents the results for C/T Ratio = Medium, our method again outperforms the Window-based analysis for sparse DAGs under all u settings. And for every edge density setting our test is better for DAG tasksets with u = Light, U sum /m > 0.3; u = Medium, U sum /m > 0.25 and u = Heavy, U sum /m > 0.15. For C/T Ratio = High, whose results are presented in Figure 5, we observe significant dominance of our LAG-based approach over the window-based approach. Like the last two settings of the C/T Ratio, our test dominates for DAG tasksets with Sparse edge density. And, for u = Light and U sum /m > 0.225 our test dominates the state-of-the-art for all edge density settings. Whereas, for u = Medium, Heavy our test performs dominates through out the U sum /m range.

Additionally, across Figures 345, comparing the combined and individual tests, we observe that even if under specific settings, the schedulability under the LAG-based analysis is lower than window-based analysis, tasksets passed by our approach are distinct from those passed by the window-based analysis. Evidence for this claim manifests across all settings in Figures 345, as a clear gap between the Combined and individual methods. Hence, our approach effectively increases the number of tasksets that can apriori be determined as schedulable working complementarily with the window-based test. Tasksets with a higher C/T Ratio and low edge density (probability of edges) are more favorable for our LAG-based utilization test. We can deduce analytical reasons for such . Figure 8 presents the results for U sum = 3.2; we can see that our approach starts to dominate the window-based under every setting. This dominance is extended to higher U sum settings of 4.0 and 4.8, as shown in Figures 9,10. For u = heavy and U sum = 4.8, both tests fail to pass any generated taskset, as shown in Figure 10c.

Similar to the first study, we see that our LAG-based approach significantly outperforms the window-based test for sparse DAG tasksets. Furthermore, the schedulability under the LAG-based test exhibits a fascinating behavior as the C/T Ratio increase beyond a threshold for higher U sum and heavier u. We observe that even under the LAG-based approach, the schedulability decreases as the C/T Ratio approaches one (See Figure 7 (b)). We can explain this behavior by analyzing the two equations that make up our LAG-based test, i.e., Eqs. 10, 11. We know that a higher C/T Ratio is favored by Eq. 11; however, as the C/T Ratio increases, the σ max of a DAG taskset also increases, making Eq. 10 fail. With large enough u and U sum , the increase in σ max overwhelming. Building an analogy to the classical density test, even though our test converts to the classical density test as C/T Ratio approaches 1, under high U sum and larger u settings the density test itself fails due to large u max leading to lower schedulability. We can observe the point where Eq. 10 overwhelms the effect of increasing C/T Ratio by comparing the threshold point where the schedulability goes down across various settings of U sum and u. For U sum = 1.6 (Figure 6), there is no threshold for u = Light, C/T Ratio ≈ 0.8 is the threshold for u = Medium and C/T Ratio ≈ 0.5 for u = Heavy. For U sum = 2.4 (Figure 7), there is still no threshold for u = Light, whereas the threshold becomes ≈ 0.65 for u = Medium and C/T Ratio < 0.4 for u = Heavy. For U sum = 3.2 (Figure 8), there is still no threshold for u = Light, and the threshold for u = Medium reduces to 0.5, and for u = Heavy, the threshold point is below 0.4. For U sum = 4.0 (Figure 9), the threshold for u = Light still does not exists and the threshold for u = Medium moves to C/T Ratio < 0.4; for u = Heavy, the threshold is somewhere below 0.4. U sum = 4.8 (Figure 10) is the first setting that a threshold point exists for u = Light, which is around 0.75; for u = Medium and heavy, the threshold is below 0.4. As discussed earlier, no schedulable tasksets exist under both the tests for u = Heavy in this U sum setting. We see the threshold point reduces with increasing U sum and u.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper presents a utilization-based schedulability test for HRT implicit deadline sporadic DAG tasksets on a multiprocessor using LAG-based analysis. We extend the apriori guarantee that we can provide for DAG tasksets. We show that our test derived from the LAG-based analysis dominates the state-of-the-art test, which uses Window-based analysis under most evaluated settings. This study further illustrates the effectiveness of LAG-based analysis in HRT systems, even though the analysis initially was intended to analyze SRT systems. Hence we urge other researchers further to explore the applicability of this novel analysis tool.
